title: The Bell That Rang Twice
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 11 of 50
content:
I woke to someone trying to be quiet.

It was an extraordinary sound.

Maui's version of quiet involved standing in the kitchen with a frying pan large enough to serve a village and arguing in a whisper with the little tattoo of himself on his chest. The tattoo pointed at the smoking pan. Maui pointed at the window. Neither appeared to consider the possibility that I might be awake.

“You're supposed to turn it over,” I said.

He froze.

Then he smiled with the solemn dignity of a demigod who had been caught burning breakfast. “Excellent. You're awake. Exactly according to my plan.”

“Your plan included smoke?”

“Atmosphere.”

I came up beside him. He had found a bowl of batter, three bananas, and an alarming quantity of honey. On the counter sat the brass key I'd carried from the shore, the blue thread newly mended. I'd left it there the night before because I was tired of sleeping with a knot digging into my skin.

Maui had put it on a folded cloth.

That, more than the disastrous pancakes, told me how careful he was trying to be.

We ate what could be saved on the front step. Tideglass Cove lay blue and still below the cliffs. A month ago I had needed someone to point me toward the next path. Now I knew the path well enough to complain about the weeds growing through its stones.

A bell rang from the vale.

One clear note.

Then another, so close behind that I thought an echo had stumbled.

Maui lowered his food.

“Does it do that?” I asked.

“No.”

His answer had lost its usual decoration.

We went inland. Neri was already standing beneath the Lanternwell's arches with a ledger open across one arm. Around her, people moved in small puzzled circles. Someone had brought a basket of seawater-soaked parcels. Someone else was carrying dry laundry that smelled faintly of the sea.

The parcels had come through the wrong doors.

“A crate of tea landed at the pier,” Neri told us. “The linen from Tideglass arrived at Jasmine Steps. Nobody's hurt, and every person who crossed went where they intended. But the things they carried didn't all follow.”

“Maybe the doors are tired,” Maui suggested.

Neri gave him a look. “Doors don't get tired.”

“I've known some very lazy doors.”

“Please don't pick a fight with the architecture.”

He put a hand over his heart. “I would never.”

The little tattoo on his chest made an unmistakable rude gesture.

I took the ledger before the argument could become a performance. On the left were the names of the districts. On the right were quantities: lamp oil, rope, medicines, grain. In the middle Neri had drawn a row of circles connected by short straight strokes.

“The bell only rang once at the festival,” I said.

“Yes.”

“What makes it ring twice?”

“I don't know.”

Neri said it without shame. That was one of the things I admired about her.

There were six doors, six approaches to the square, and six brass rings around the mechanism beneath the spring. The seventh circle in her diagram wasn't a door at all. It was an empty place in the center, marked with a dot.

“The space for what we owe one another,” she said when she saw where I was looking.

“That's cheerful.”

“It's practical.”

Neri explained that each district kept its own promises. If the pier borrowed canvas, someone at the pier returned it or accounted for the loss. If the archive sent a book across, the borrower signed it back in. The well's old keepers had treated these arrangements as merely social.

Then the first misdelivery had happened.

“I need to look at the mechanism,” I said.

Maui was already rolling his shoulders. “Stand aside. One heroic lift and the problem is solved.”

“Please don't lift a magical spring out of the ground.”

“You're putting very unreasonable limits on heroism.”

Neri handed me a lantern. Maui carried tools because he insisted, not because he was the only person strong enough. Beneath the arches, a stair followed damp stone into a chamber scarcely taller than my shoulders. Maui had to duck. It delighted me.

Six little brass wheels turned under a narrow channel of running water. Each wheel held a notch shaped to meet its neighbor. Above them hung a seventh ring, entirely still.

One tooth on the wheel marked STARWAKE had been bent.

“That,” I said, “is either a very small problem or a very large one.”

“Can you fix it?” Maui asked.

“I can tell you how it broke.”

The wheels had been trying to carry more than the mechanism was designed to track. Not people; the Threadways still recognized a person's decision to cross. Cargo, though—everyone's generous bundles, borrowed tools, baskets pushed over thresholds without a receipt—had made a confusion of responsibilities.

Neri rubbed her forehead. “We thought gifts were different from loans.”

“They are,” I said. “But somebody still has to know where they ended up.”

Maui crouched until we were eye to eye. The cramped chamber forced the boastfulness out of his posture.

“Okay, little inventor. Tell me what you need.”

I liked the way he said it. Not because it made me his. Because he asked what I could do, and waited.

“First, nobody lifts anything. Second, we tell the others. Third, you promise not to call this the Great Bell Incident until somebody decides whether that's a good name.”

He opened his mouth.

“Maui.”

“Fine. The Moderately Impressive Bell Inconvenience.”

I laughed, which was irritating because it rewarded him.

Then the seventh ring moved.

Only a fraction.

It sounded like a spoon striking the edge of a cup.

Above us the well rang three times, and the water in the channel flowed backward.

Maui caught my elbow. I caught the lantern. Neri caught the ledger, which told me everything I needed to know about our priorities.

No one was pulled through a door. No memory returned. No great prophecy spoke.

A thin line of salt appeared across the stone floor.

I knew that salt.

I had walked through it on the morning I found my name.

Maui looked from the line to me. For once he did not ask whether I remembered more.

He asked, “What do you want to do?”

I stared at the old blue thread around my key. Then I looked at the ledger and the bent brass tooth, two ordinary things stubbornly refusing to be mystical enough to excuse our mistakes.

“We make a list,” I said. “Then we invite everyone who has a door to help us understand it.”

“And breakfast?”

“You ruined breakfast.”

“I can make another.”

I caught the edge of his hand as we climbed. He turned toward me, his smile returning slowly.

“Later,” I said. “And you can kiss me after you wash that honey off your fingers.”

He bent close enough that I could feel his warmth against my cheek. “The great Maui does not take orders.”

“Then the great Maui can sleep alone.”

He washed his hands.

By noon, notices were hanging at every threshold. At the top, in Neri's careful script, was a sentence we agreed should not need magic to be true:

NOTHING BORROWED IS INVISIBLE.

Beneath it I added: NEITHER IS ANYONE'S CHOICE.

The bell remained silent for the rest of the day.

I found that considerably less reassuring than I had expected.
